blocks.context: For example, Fatima runs a tailoring shop in Ilorin and has about three hours a week for content.
steps: Sunday, 30 minutes: she writes three ideas: a new kaftan style (Products), "How to measure your bust correctly" (Education), and a Reel of a dress being finished (Behind the scenes).
Monday, 60 minutes at 10am by the shop window: she photographs the kaftan on a mannequin, films the 1-minute measuring tip, and films clips of the finishing work.
Tuesday, 60 minutes: she makes the product post from her Canva master, edits the tip video and the Reel in CapCut, and writes three captions.
Tuesday, 15 minutes: she schedules the three posts in Meta Business Suite for Wednesday, Friday and Saturday evenings.
Saturday, 15 minutes: she notes results in her sheet; the measuring tip got 14 saves and 6 messages asking for appointments (her own illustrative numbers).
blocks.result: Three quality posts go out in a steady rhythm for about three hours of work, and her sheet shows that education posts bring enquiries, so she plans one tip every week.

blocks.title: Keep an ideas list
blocks.text: Whenever a customer asks a question, add it to an ideas note on your phone. Real customer questions are the best source of education posts and short videos.

takeaways: Three to five content pillars keep your posts varied and on topic.
Post steadily at a pace you can keep; three good posts a week is a solid start.
Batch planning, shooting, designing and scheduling to save time.
Track results weekly and make more of what brings messages and sales.

activity.title: Plan and batch one week of content
steps: Write your three to five content pillars.
Create a calendar for next week with at least three posts and daily status ideas.
Shoot all the photos and clips in one session.
Design and edit all posts in one session using your templates.
Schedule or post them and record results at the end of the week.
activity.evidence: Your calendar (photo or screenshot) and your results sheet after one week.

lessons.title: Using AI tools safely: ideas, captions and images with a human check
objectives: Use an AI chat assistant to brainstorm ideas and draft captions
Use AI features in Canva and CapCut for speed
Check AI output for errors, made-up facts and tone
Protect customer data and be honest about AI images

blocks.text: **Generative AI** tools create text, images, audio or video from your instructions, called **prompts**. Well known examples are chat assistants such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Claude, plus AI features inside Canva (such as Magic Write for text and Magic Media for images) and CapCut (such as auto captions). Used well, AI saves time on first drafts. Used carelessly, it produces generic content, wrong facts and images that mislead customers. The rule for this lesson is simple: **AI drafts, you decide**.

blocks.name: chat-with-ai
blocks.alt: A person chatting with an AI assistant
blocks.caption: AI can give you a fast first draft, but you remain the editor.

blocks.text: Writing a good prompt
AI gives much better results when you give it context. A useful prompt includes five parts: **who you are, who the audience is, what you want, the format, and the tone**. Compare these two:

head: Weak prompt
Strong prompt
rows: "I run a home bakery in Ibadan. Write three Instagram captions, each under 50 words, for a red velvet birthday cake costing about 25,000 naira. Audience: mothers planning children's parties. Tone: warm and simple. End each with 'Send a DM to order'."
"Give me 10 short video ideas for a tailoring shop in Ilorin, grouped under these pillars: products, tips, behind the scenes. One line each."

blocks.text: Good uses of AI for a content creator

items: Brainstorming lists of post ideas and hooks.
Drafting captions, which you then rewrite in your own voice.
Turning a long voice note or article into short bullet points.
Translating a caption into Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or Pidgin as a draft, then checking it with a fluent speaker, because AI translation of Nigerian languages can be wrong.
Generating auto captions for videos in CapCut, then proofreading them.
Creating simple background images or illustrations for designs where a real photo is not needed.

blocks.text: What to check every time

AI tools can state things that sound confident but are false; this is often called **hallucination**. Check every fact, price, date, law or health statement yourself. Read the tone: AI often sounds stiff or too excited for a Nigerian audience, so rewrite it to sound like you. Remove phrases you would never say. Look closely at AI images for wrong hands, strange text, or cultural details that look wrong.
Building a reusable prompt

Once a prompt works well, save it in a phone note and reuse it, changing only the product details. You can also start a conversation by pasting your brand guide in words: business name, location, audience, three personality words, and words you never use. Then every answer in that conversation starts closer to your style. Ask for several options at once and choose the best, rather than accepting the first answer.

blocks.title: AI with a human check
items: Write a clear prompt
Get an AI draft
Check facts and tone
Rewrite in your voice
Publish
blocks.caption: The human check between draft and publish is the step that protects your reputation.

blocks.text: Honesty and privacy

items: **Never show AI images as real products or real results.** If customers buy based on an AI picture, they will be disappointed and may report you. Use real photos for products.

**Do not paste private data** such as customers' names, phone numbers, addresses or account details into AI tools. Many tools may use what you type to improve their systems unless you change settings.
**Do not create images of real people** without their consent, and never create fake endorsements.
Read each tool's terms on commercial use before using AI images in ads or for sale.

blocks.title: Worked example: drafting a week of captions with AI
blocks.context: For example, Folake sells handmade beaded bags in Abeokuta and wants captions for three posts.
steps: She types a strong prompt: who she is, the three bags (prices about 15,000, 18,500 and 22,000 naira), the audience (women going to owambe parties), tone (friendly, short), and the action ("WhatsApp to order").
The AI returns nine captions. She picks three she likes.
She checks facts: one caption said the bags were "waterproof"; they are not, so she deletes that line.
She rewrites each caption in her own words, adding a Yoruba greeting she would really use.
She does not paste her customer list or phone contacts into the tool.
blocks.result: She finishes three captions in about 15 minutes instead of an hour, with no false claims, and they still sound like her.

blocks.title: Label AI images when it matters
blocks.text: If you use an AI image for a mood or background, such as a festive pattern, that is fine. If an image could be mistaken for a real event, product or person, say it is AI generated in the caption.

blocks.title: AI scams
blocks.text: Be careful of apps and ads promising AI that will "make you rich" or "run your page for you" for an upfront fee. Use well-known tools from their official websites or app stores, and never share your social media passwords with a third-party tool.

takeaways: AI drafts, you decide: always edit and check before publishing.
Good prompts include who you are, audience, task, format and tone.
Check every fact; AI can confidently make things up.
Use real photos for products, and never paste private customer data into AI tools.

activity.title: Draft and edit with AI
steps: Write a strong prompt for captions or ideas for your business using the five parts.
Run it in an AI assistant you can access.
Highlight every fact in the output and check each one.
Rewrite your favourite result in your own voice.
Save the prompt, the AI draft and your final version side by side.
activity.evidence: A screenshot or note showing your prompt, the AI draft and your edited final caption.

lessons.title: Smartphone photography with natural light
objectives: Use window light and outdoor shade for clear, flattering photos
Compose photos with the rule of thirds, clean backgrounds and good angles
Take product, food and portrait photos for business use
Edit photos lightly on the phone without making them look fake

blocks.text: Photos are the backbone of your content: products, food, finished work, team and customers. Good light is the biggest difference between a dull photo and a professional one, and the best light is free: **daylight**. In this lesson you learn to find and use natural light, compose photos, and edit them lightly on your phone.

blocks.name: camera-with-flash
blocks.caption: Daylight from a window often beats the flash for product and portrait photos.

blocks.text: Understanding natural light

items: **Window light**: place your subject beside a window, with light coming from the side. This gives soft, shaped light. Avoid windows with direct sun streaming in, or cover them with a thin white curtain to soften it.
**Open shade**: outdoors, stand in the shade of a building or tree, facing the open sky. Skin looks even, with no harsh shadows.
**Golden hour**: the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset give warm, soft light, lovely for portraits and outdoor products.
**Avoid midday overhead sun**: it creates dark eye shadows and shiny spots.
**Avoid the phone flash** for most business photos; it flattens the subject and causes harsh shadows and red eyes.

blocks.text: A **reflector** bounces light back into shadows. You do not need to buy one: a sheet of white cardboard, a white bedsheet or even aluminium foil on card, held on the side opposite the window, lifts dark shadows.
Composition basics

items: **Rule of thirds**: turn on gridlines and place your subject on one of the lines or where two lines cross, not always in the dead centre.
**Clean background**: remove clutter. A plain wall, a cloth, or a wooden board makes the product stand out.
**Fill the frame**: walk closer instead of using digital zoom.
**Angles**: shoot flat items such as plated food or fabrics from directly above; shoot tall items such as bottles and bags straight on at their own height; shoot people at eye level.
**Leading lines**: roads, tables and shelves can guide the eye towards the subject.

blocks.text: Three photo types every business needs

head: Type
Set up
Tip
rows: Plain background, window light from the side, white card reflector
Take a front, side, detail and in-use photo of each product
Near a window, top down or 45 degrees, clean plate edges
Shoot quickly while food is fresh; wipe drips
Face the window or stand in open shade; use portrait mode
Use the 2x lens if your phone has one, to avoid stretched faces

blocks.text: Light editing on your phone

Use the built-in editor in your gallery app or a free app such as Snapseed (by Google). A good order is: **crop and straighten** first, then **exposure or brightness**, then **contrast**, then **warmth**, and only a small amount of **saturation**. Keep skin tones natural and product colours true; if a customer receives a fabric that looks different from your photo, you lose trust. Avoid heavy beauty filters on product or service photos.
Keeping photos consistent

Use the same background, angle and time of day for a product range so your catalogue looks like one set. Take photos in the highest quality setting your phone offers, and keep the unedited originals in a separate album. WhatsApp compresses photos it sends; to share a full-quality photo with a printer or designer, send it as a document instead of as an image.

blocks.title: Window light vs flash
items: Side window light
Phone flash
blocks.caption: Side window light shapes the subject softly, while flash flattens it.

blocks.title: Worked example: a product photo setup for beaded bags
blocks.context: For example, Folake from Lesson 4.2 needs photos of her beaded bags for her catalogue and Instagram.
steps: At 10am she puts a small table beside her north-facing window, where light is bright but the sun does not shine directly in.
She tapes a cream cloth to the wall and lays it over the table to create a seamless background.
She places a bag on the table and holds a white cardboard sheet on the side opposite the window to soften shadows.
She turns on gridlines, puts the bag on the right third line, taps it to focus and slides exposure slightly down so the white beads keep detail.
She takes four photos: front, side, close-up of the beadwork and a hand holding the bag.
In Snapseed she straightens, brightens slightly and adds a little contrast, keeping colours true.
blocks.result: Clean, consistent catalogue photos with true colours, made in about 30 minutes with a window, a cloth and a piece of cardboard.

blocks.title: Permission for people
blocks.text: Ask before photographing customers, and get clear permission before posting their faces, especially children. Some people do not want to appear online for privacy or safety reasons.

takeaways: Daylight from the side of a window or open shade gives the best free light.
Use white card as a reflector and avoid the flash for business photos.
Use gridlines and the rule of thirds; clean the background and walk closer instead of zooming.
Edit lightly and keep product colours true.

activity.title: Shoot a product set with window light
steps: Pick one product or dish.
Set up beside a window with a plain background and a white card reflector.
Take front, side, detail and in-use photos using gridlines.
Take one more photo with the flash on to compare.
Edit your best photo lightly and keep the original too.
activity.evidence: The four natural-light photos, the flash comparison photo and your edited best photo.

lessons.title: Repurposing, distribution and copyright-safe images
objectives: Turn one core piece of content into several formats
Share content on WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook and other platforms in the right way
Find images you are legally allowed to use
Understand Creative Commons licences and give proper credit

blocks.text: Creating new content takes time. **Repurposing** means taking one strong piece of content and turning it into several formats for different platforms. One 60-second tip video can become a Reel, a WhatsApp Status series, a carousel, a caption and a voice note. This lesson also covers where your content goes (distribution) and how to use images from others without breaking copyright.

blocks.name: share-everywhere
blocks.alt: Content being shared across many platforms
blocks.caption: One strong idea can be shared in many formats across many platforms.

blocks.text: The repurposing tree
Start with one **core piece** that has the most information, often a video or a voice recording where you explain something properly. Then cut it into smaller pieces:

items: **Short video**: trim the best 20 to 30 seconds for Reels, Shorts and TikTok.
**Status series**: split the video into short clips for WhatsApp Status.
**Carousel**: turn the main points into 5 slides using your Canva master template.
**Quote graphic**: take the most useful sentence and put it on a branded square.
**Caption or article**: write the points out as a caption, a Facebook post or a WhatsApp broadcast message.
**Audio**: share the sound only as a voice note for listeners with little data.

blocks.title: One idea, many formats
items: Core video or audio
Short vertical clip
Carousel and quote graphic
Caption and broadcast text
blocks.caption: Start from the richest piece and cut it down into lighter formats.

blocks.text: Distribution: where and how

head: Channel
Best use
rows: Daily updates to people who saved your number
WhatsApp Business catalogue and broadcast lists
Product photos with prices; messages to customers who agreed to receive them
Discovery by new people through Reels, posts and hashtags
Reaching new audiences with short videos
Professional services, partnerships, NGO and corporate audiences

blocks.text: Adjust each piece to its platform: vertical for Status and Reels, square or portrait for feed posts, more formal words for LinkedIn. Do not post a video with another app's watermark on a competing platform; download your original from CapCut or your gallery instead.
Copyright: what you may use

**Copyright** protects photos, music, videos, designs and writing from the moment they are created. In Nigeria, copyright is governed by the Copyright Act 2022 and administered by the Nigerian Copyright Commission. In plain terms: **a photo found on Google or someone's Instagram is not free to use** just because you can download it. Using it in your business posts can lead to takedowns, account strikes or legal claims.
Safe sources of images

head: Source
What the licence generally allows
Credit needed?
rows: Anything, as long as people in them agreed
Use inside your Canva designs, under Canva's content licence; do not resell the images alone or trademark them
Free to use, including commercially, under their own licences; do not sell unaltered copies or imply endorsement
Depends on each file's licence, often Creative Commons
Usually yes, follow the file's licence
Mostly copyrighted; not a safe source

blocks.text: Creative Commons in brief

**Creative Commons (CC)** licences let creators share work with clear conditions. **BY** means you must credit the creator. **SA** (ShareAlike) means your new work must use the same licence. **NC** (NonCommercial) means no business use. **ND** (NoDerivatives) means you may not change it. **CC0** means the creator has given up rights, so you may use it freely. For a business post, avoid NC images. A good credit looks like: "Photo: Name, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons".

Copyright also covers music and video. Using a popular song in a business video, or reposting someone else's video without permission, can get your post muted or removed. Reposting with credit is not the same as permission; ask the creator first and keep their written reply.

blocks.title: Worked example: repurposing one tip video and choosing a safe image
blocks.context: For example, Joy the hair stylist from Lesson 3.3 has a 90-second video explaining braid aftercare.
steps: She trims the best 28 seconds into a Reel and posts it on Instagram and Facebook.
She splits the full video into three 30-second clips for WhatsApp Status across one day.
She turns the three tips into a 5-slide Canva carousel and a single quote graphic: "Satin at night protects your edges".
She needs a background image of a satin scarf for the quote graphic. She does not take one from Google; she uses a free Canva photo without a crown.
She writes one WhatsApp broadcast message summarising the tips and sends it only to customers who agreed to receive updates.
blocks.result: One recording becomes six pieces of content across four channels in about an hour, all using images she is allowed to use.

blocks.title: When in doubt, leave it out
blocks.text: If you cannot find a clear licence for an image or song, do not use it for business. Take your own photo, use Canva's free library, or use Unsplash or Pexels and keep a screenshot of the licence page for your records.

takeaways: Start with one rich core piece and cut it into lighter formats.
Adapt each piece to its platform; avoid other apps' watermarks.
Images from Google or other people's pages are usually copyrighted.
Use your own photos, Canva free items, Unsplash, Pexels or correctly credited Creative Commons images.

activity.title: Repurpose one piece of content
steps: Choose your best video or audio from this course.
Turn it into at least four formats: short clip, status clips, carousel and caption.
For any image you did not create, note its source and licence.
Post or schedule the pieces on at least two different channels.
Record which format got the most response.
activity.evidence: A list of the four or more pieces with where each was posted, and the source and licence of any borrowed image.

quiz.q: Bola posts every day for a week, then stops for a month. What would help most?
options: A realistic weekly calendar with batching, such as three posts a week
quiz.explain: A steady pace she can keep, supported by batching, beats bursts followed by silence.

quiz.q: An AI tool writes a caption saying Grace's soap is "NAFDAC approved", but she has no NAFDAC number. What should she do?
options: Delete the false claim before posting
Ask the AI to make it sound more confident
quiz.explain: AI can invent facts. Only true claims should be published, and NAFDAC claims require a real registration.

quiz.q: Which light is best for a beaded bag product photo indoors?
options: Soft daylight from the side of a window, with white card as reflector
Direct midday sun through the window
quiz.explain: Side window light gives soft, true-colour light, and the reflector lifts shadows.

quiz.q: Which image can Ada safely use in a business flyer?
options: A photo copied from a famous brand's Instagram
A Google Images result with no licence shown
A free Pexels photo used under its licence
quiz.explain: Pexels images are free for commercial use under its licence. NC licences forbid commercial use, and random web images are usually copyrighted.

quiz.q: What does CC BY require?
options: You cannot use it at all
You must not change anything about it
quiz.explain: BY means attribution: credit the creator as the licence asks.

quiz.q: Joy has one 90-second tip video. Which plan is the best example of repurposing?
options: Make a Reel, status clips, a carousel and a broadcast message from it
Post the same 90-second file everywhere once
Delete it and make a new video for each platform
quiz.explain: Repurposing adapts one core piece into several formats suited to each platform.

finalQuiz.q: Which three design rules fix most cluttered flyers?
options: More fonts, more colours, more photos
Centred text, all caps and borders
finalQuiz.explain: Contrast makes text readable, alignment makes it tidy, and hierarchy tells the eye what to read first.

finalQuiz.q: Amaka records her brand colours as #C8102E and #F2A900. What are these?
finalQuiz.explain: HEX codes identify exact colours so they can be used consistently in Canva, CapCut and elsewhere.

finalQuiz.q: Which download format should Halima use for a text-heavy price list going to WhatsApp?
finalQuiz.explain: PNG keeps text and edges sharp for digital graphics.

finalQuiz.q: What size should a WhatsApp Status or Instagram Story design be?
finalQuiz.explain: Stories and Status use the 9:16 vertical size of 1080 x 1920 pixels.

finalQuiz.q: Grace wants to show how members' savings grew each quarter. Which is the most honest choice?
options: A bar chart starting at zero with units and source labelled
A bar chart starting at 300,000 to look dramatic
A chart without labels to keep it clean
finalQuiz.explain: Bars starting at zero with clear units and source give a truthful comparison.

finalQuiz.q: Esther's LinkedIn banner text is hidden behind her profile photo. Where should key text go?
options: Towards the right and centre of the 1584 x 396 banner
finalQuiz.explain: The profile photo covers the lower left on many screens, so keep text right of centre.

finalQuiz.q: Before filming, which step costs nothing and most improves sharpness?
finalQuiz.explain: A greasy lens makes footage hazy; cleaning it is free and immediate.

finalQuiz.q: In CapCut, which order of work avoids redoing captions?
options: Trim and arrange clips, then add text and captions, then export
Add captions first, then rearrange clips
Add music, then delete clips randomly
finalQuiz.explain: Captions are tied to timing, so finish arranging clips before adding them.

finalQuiz.q: A 30-second Reel script should contain roughly how many spoken words?
finalQuiz.explain: At 2 to 3 words per second, 30 seconds holds about 60 to 80 words.

finalQuiz.q: Blessing's audio has fan hum and echo. What should she do?
options: Move the phone a metre away
Turn off the fan and record in a room with soft furnishings
finalQuiz.explain: Removing noise sources and using soft rooms solves hum and echo at the source.

finalQuiz.q: Folake asks AI for captions and it says her bags are waterproof, which is untrue. What is the correct next step?
options: Ask the AI to repeat the claim louder
Add a disclaimer that AI wrote it
Remove the false claim and rewrite in her own voice
finalQuiz.explain: AI can invent facts. The human check removes false claims before anything is published.

finalQuiz.q: Which image is safest for a business advert?
options: Her own photo taken with permission of anyone in it
A screenshot of a competitor's post
finalQuiz.explain: Your own photo, with consent from people shown, is the safest. NC licences forbid commercial use, and web images are usually copyrighted.

capstone.title: Content Creation Portfolio: one week of branded content
capstone.brief: Produce a complete one-week content package for a real business, group or cause: a brand guide, four designed graphics, one edited short video, one audio tip and a content calendar with results, all using images and music you are allowed to use.
steps: Create a one-page brand guide with three personality words, HEX colours, two fonts and a text-based logo.
Design four graphics in Canva: a product or announcement post (1080 x 1350), a five-slide carousel, a story (1080 x 1920) and either an infographic or a professional document.
Take a set of four natural-light product or service photos and edit your best one lightly.
Script, film and edit a 20 to 30 second vertical video in CapCut with a hook, captions and correctly licensed music.
Record a 2-minute audio tip in a quiet room.
Plan the week in a content calendar, post or schedule the pieces, and record results after seven days.
Write a short note listing the source and licence of any image or music you did not create.
evidence: Four graphic files at the correct sizes
Image and music source and licence list
